questiontext.text: Predicate Coverage (PC) requires that:

answer.text: Each predicate in the program evaluates to both true and false

feedback.text: Correct.

answer.text: Each clause within a predicate evaluates to both true and false

feedback.text: That's Clause Coverage (CC).

answer.text: All combinations of clause truth values are exercised for each predicate

feedback.text: That's Combinatorial Coverage (CoC).

answer.text: Every path through the predicate's decision structure is exercised

feedback.text: That describes Path Coverage, not Predicate Coverage.

generalfeedback.text: Predicate Coverage (PC) only requires the whole predicate to take both truth values at least once; it says nothing about the individual clauses inside it — that finer-grained requirement is Clause Coverage.

questiontext.text: In logic coverage, a clause is:

answer.text: A boolean expression that contains no boolean operators

feedback.text: Correct — a clause is an atomic condition such as x > 0 or a boolean variable.

answer.text: Any boolean expression, however it is built from operators

feedback.text: That is a predicate; a clause is the atomic building block with no boolean operators.

answer.text: A complete if-statement in the source code

feedback.text: A clause is a condition, not a whole statement.

answer.text: A test case that exercises one branch

feedback.text: That is a test, not a clause.

generalfeedback.text: A clause (or condition) is a boolean expression containing no boolean operators (&&, ||, !). Predicates are built by connecting clauses with boolean operators.

questiontext.text: Which expression is a predicate built from exactly three clauses?

feedback.text: Correct — the clauses are a, b, and c, joined by boolean operators.
That is a single clause, not a predicate over three clauses.
That predicate has only two clauses.
That is an arithmetic expression, not a boolean predicate.

generalfeedback.text: A predicate is a boolean expression built from clauses connected by boolean operators. (a && b) || c has three clauses (a, b, c).

questiontext.text: Clause Coverage (CC) requires that:

answer.text: Each clause in each predicate evaluates to both true and false

feedback.text: Correct — every individual clause must take on both truth values.

answer.text: Each predicate evaluates to both true and false

feedback.text: That is Predicate Coverage (PC), which looks at the whole predicate.

answer.text: All combinations of clause values are exercised

feedback.text: That is Combinatorial Coverage (CoC).

answer.text: Each clause determines its predicate at least once

feedback.text: That is the active-clause idea (ACC), stronger than plain Clause Coverage.

generalfeedback.text: Clause Coverage requires each clause to be both true and false at least once, independently of what the enclosing predicate does.

questiontext.text: A predicate has 3 independent clauses. How many tests does Combinatorial Coverage (CoC) require?

feedback.text: Correct — 2^3 combinations of true/false.
That's roughly the size of Clause Coverage (one flip per clause), not every combination.
Too few — 4 tests can't realize all 8 truth-value combinations.
6 falls short of the full 2^3 = 8 combinations.

generalfeedback.text: Combinatorial Coverage requires every one of the 2^n truth-value combinations of n clauses to be exercised (subject to feasibility); with 3 independent clauses that is 2^3 = 8 tests.

questiontext.text: How many rows are in the full truth table of a predicate with 2 clauses (the number Combinatorial Coverage requires)?

feedback.text: Correct — 2^2 = 4 combinations.
2 is the count for Predicate or Clause Coverage, not every combination.
8 = 2^3 would be three clauses, not two.

generalfeedback.text: A predicate with n clauses has 2^n truth-table rows; for n = 2 that is 4.

questiontext.text: A predicate has 4 independent clauses. How many tests does Combinatorial Coverage (CoC) require?

feedback.text: Correct — 2^4 = 16 combinations.
8 = 2^3 would be three clauses.
5 = n+1 is the minimal count for CACC/MC-DC, not CoC.
4 is the number of clauses, not the number of combinations.

generalfeedback.text: Combinatorial Coverage needs all 2^n rows; for n = 4 that is 2^4 = 16 tests.

name.text: Satisfying rows of a AND b

questiontext.text: For the predicate a && b, how many of the 4 possible assignments make it true?

feedback.text: Correct — only a=T, b=T satisfies a conjunction.
Only the all-true row satisfies a && b.
3 is the count for a || b, not a && b.
A conjunction is false whenever any clause is false, so not all 4 rows satisfy it.

generalfeedback.text: A conjunction is true only when every clause is true, so exactly 1 of the 4 rows satisfies a && b.

name.text: Satisfying rows of a OR b

questiontext.text: For the predicate a || b, how many of the 4 possible assignments make it true?

feedback.text: Correct — only a=F, b=F fails, leaving 3 satisfying rows.
1 is the count for a && b, not a || b.
A disjunction fails only on the all-false row, so 3 rows satisfy it.
The all-false row (a=F, b=F) does not satisfy a || b.

generalfeedback.text: A disjunction is false only when every clause is false, so 3 of the 4 rows satisfy a || b.

name.text: Satisfying rows of (a AND b) OR c

questiontext.text: For the predicate (a && b) || c over 3 clauses, how many of the 8 possible assignments make it true?

feedback.text: Correct — 4 rows with c=T, plus the single row a=T,b=T,c=F.
The 4 rows with c=T all satisfy it, but the row a=T,b=T,c=F does too, giving 5.
Recount — exactly 5 of the 8 rows are true.
Too few — c=T alone already gives 4 true rows.

generalfeedback.text: Whenever c=T the predicate is true (4 rows); when c=F it needs a=T and b=T (1 more row). Total = 5 of 8.

name.text: Satisfying rows of a OR b OR c

questiontext.text: For the predicate a || b || c, how many of the 8 possible assignments make it true?

feedback.text: Correct — only the all-false row fails, leaving 7.
The all-false row a=F,b=F,c=F does not satisfy it.
Only one row (all false) fails, so 7 satisfy it.
1 would be a conjunction; a disjunction is true on 7 of 8 rows.

generalfeedback.text: A three-way disjunction is false only on the single all-false row, so 7 of 8 rows satisfy a || b || c.

questiontext.text: What is the minimum number of tests needed to satisfy Predicate Coverage for a single predicate?

feedback.text: Correct — one test making the predicate true and one making it false.
One test can only give one truth value; PC needs both.
n+1 is the minimum for CACC/MC-DC, not Predicate Coverage.
2^n is Combinatorial Coverage, far more than PC needs.

generalfeedback.text: Predicate Coverage needs the predicate to be true once and false once — a minimum of 2 tests, regardless of how many clauses it has.

questiontext.text: A predicate has 3 independent clauses. What is the minimum number of tests that can satisfy Clause Coverage?

feedback.text: Correct — one all-true test and one all-false test make every clause both true and false.
You do not need one test per clause; 2 tests can flip all clauses together.
Clause Coverage is about each clause taking both values, achievable in 2 tests.
8 = 2^3 is Combinatorial Coverage, not Clause Coverage.

generalfeedback.text: Setting all clauses true in one test and all false in another gives every clause both values, so Clause Coverage needs only 2 tests (for independent clauses), independent of clause count.

questiontext.text: By definition, a clause contains no boolean operators (such as &&, ||, or !).

feedback.text: Correct — a clause is an atomic boolean expression with no boolean operators.
A clause is defined precisely as a boolean expression with no boolean operators; adding operators makes it a predicate.

generalfeedback.text: A clause (condition) is a boolean expression containing no boolean operators. Connecting clauses with &&/||/! produces a predicate.

name.text: Satisfying rows of a AND b AND c

questiontext.text: For the predicate a && b && c, how many of the 8 possible assignments make it true?

feedback.text: Correct — only the all-true row satisfies a three-way conjunction.
A conjunction is true only when every clause is true — just 1 row.
7 is the count for a || b || c, the disjunction.
The all-true row (a=T,b=T,c=T) does satisfy it.

generalfeedback.text: A conjunction is true only when all clauses are true, so exactly 1 of the 8 rows satisfies a && b && c.

questiontext.text: For predicate p = a ∧ b, clause a determines p exactly when:

feedback.text: Correct — with b true, p's value is exactly a's value, so toggling a toggles p.
When b is false, p is false regardless of a, so a cannot determine p.
Determination is a per-clause, per-assignment condition, not a constant.
Conjunctions do have determining assignments — just not when b is false.

generalfeedback.text: A clause c determines predicate p when changing only c's truth value changes p's truth value while the other clauses stay fixed. For p = a ∧ b, that happens exactly when b = true: p then mirrors a exactly.

questiontext.text: How does Restricted Active Clause Coverage (RACC) differ from Correlated Active Clause Coverage (CACC)?

answer.text: RACC additionally requires the minor clauses to hold identical values in the true/false test pair for the major clause

feedback.text: Correct — RACC is the stricter, "same minor-clause values" version of CACC.

answer.text: RACC drops the requirement that the major clause determines the predicate

feedback.text: That describes General Active Clause Coverage (GACC), not RACC.

answer.text: RACC only counts inactive clauses, not active ones

feedback.text: That describes the inactive-clause family (GICC/RICC), not RACC.

answer.text: RACC requires covering all combinations of clause values

feedback.text: That's Combinatorial Coverage (CoC).

generalfeedback.text: Both criteria require, for each major clause ci, a pair of tests where ci determines predicate p once true and once false. CACC allows the other (minor) clauses to differ between that pair; RACC additionally pins the minor clauses to the same values across the pair, making it strictly stronger.

questiontext.text: A clause c determines a predicate p (for a given assignment of the other clauses) when:

answer.text: Toggling only c, with the other clauses fixed, changes the value of p

feedback.text: Correct — c controls p's outcome given the fixed minor clauses.

answer.text: c and p always have the same truth value

feedback.text: Determination is about c controlling p when toggled, not about them being equal.
Appearing in p is necessary but not sufficient; c must actually control the outcome.

answer.text: p is true whenever c is true

feedback.text: That is one special case, not the general definition of determination.

generalfeedback.text: c determines p under a fixed assignment of the minor clauses if flipping c (and nothing else) flips p. This is the key precondition for active-clause criteria.

questiontext.text: General Active Clause Coverage (GACC) requires, for each major clause ci:

answer.text: Two tests in which ci is true and false while ci determines p; the minor clauses may take any values

feedback.text: Correct — GACC is the most permissive active-clause criterion about minor clauses.

answer.text: Two tests in which the minor clauses hold identical values

feedback.text: That extra restriction is RACC, not GACC.

answer.text: Two tests in which p is true and false

feedback.text: Requiring p to differ is CACC; GACC does not require it.
That is Combinatorial Coverage.

generalfeedback.text: GACC requires, for each major clause, a true test and a false test in which that clause determines the predicate. It places no constraint on the minor clauses and does not require p itself to differ across the pair.

questiontext.text: For predicate p = a ∨ b, clause a determines p exactly when:

feedback.text: Correct — with b false, p equals a, so toggling a toggles p.
When b is true, p is true regardless of a, so a cannot determine p.
a fails to determine p when b is true.
Disjunctions do have determining assignments — when the other clause is false.

generalfeedback.text: For p = a ∨ b, a determines p exactly when b = false: then p mirrors a. When b is true, p is fixed true and a is irrelevant. (Dually for a ∧ b, a determines p when b is true.)

questiontext.text: What does Correlated Active Clause Coverage (CACC) require that General Active Clause Coverage (GACC) does not?

answer.text: The predicate p must be true in one test of the pair and false in the other

feedback.text: Correct — CACC correlates the major clause's flip with a change in p.

answer.text: The minor clauses must be identical across the pair

feedback.text: That extra requirement defines RACC, not CACC.

answer.text: Every clause combination must be tested

feedback.text: That is Combinatorial Coverage.

answer.text: The major clause need not determine p

feedback.text: All active-clause criteria require determination.

generalfeedback.text: GACC only requires the major clause to be true and false while determining p; CACC additionally requires p itself to take both values across the pair. Because of this, CACC subsumes Predicate Coverage while GACC does not.

questiontext.text: For a predicate with n independent clauses, what is the minimum number of tests that can satisfy CACC (MC/DC)?

feedback.text: Correct — MC/DC can be satisfied with as few as n+1 well-chosen tests.
2n is an upper bound (a pair per clause), not the achievable minimum.
2^n is Combinatorial Coverage, far more than MC/DC needs.
2 suffices for Predicate Coverage, but MC/DC needs to exercise each clause independently.

generalfeedback.text: By sharing tests across clauses, CACC/MC-DC for n independent clauses can be met with a minimum of n+1 tests (and at most 2n).

questiontext.text: In active clause coverage, when we test whether clause ci determines the predicate, ci is called the major clause and the others are:

feedback.text: Correct — the remaining clauses are the minor clauses for that requirement.
They are clauses, not predicates, and this is not the standard term.
Determination is the property being tested; the fixed clauses are the minor clauses.
The standard terminology is major/minor clauses.

generalfeedback.text: Active-clause criteria pick one clause as the major clause (whose determination is tested) and treat the rest as minor clauses, whose values are set to let the major clause determine the predicate.

questiontext.text: What is the subsumption relationship between Predicate Coverage (PC) and Clause Coverage (CC)?

feedback.text: Correct — CC can leave the predicate one-valued, and PC can leave a clause one-valued.
Making each clause both values need not make the whole predicate take both values.
Making the predicate both values need not flip every individual clause.
They are incomparable, not equivalent.

generalfeedback.text: PC and CC are incomparable: neither subsumes the other. (For example, with p = a ∧ b, tests a=T,b=T and a=F,b=T satisfy PC but never make b false; other test sets satisfy CC without making p both values.)

name.text: Determination of c in (a AND b) OR c

questiontext.text: For predicate p = (a ∧ b) ∨ c, clause c determines p exactly when:

feedback.text: Correct — when (a ∧ b) is false, p equals c; when it is true, p is true regardless of c.
Then p is true no matter what c is, so c does not determine p.
a alone does not fix whether c matters; the condition is on the whole term a ∧ b.
c cannot determine p when a ∧ b is already true.

generalfeedback.text: For a disjunction p = X ∨ c, clause c determines p exactly when the other operand X is false. Here X = a ∧ b, so c determines p when a ∧ b is false.

name.text: Active clause count at a row

questiontext.text: For the predicate (a || b) && c evaluated at a=T, b=F, c=T, how many of the 3 clauses are active (flipping that clause alone changes the predicate's value)?

feedback.text: Correct — flipping a (T→F makes a||b false) or c (T→F) changes p; flipping b does not.
Both a and c are active here; b is not.
Flipping b (F→T) leaves a||b true, so p is unchanged; b is not active.
At least a and c change the outcome when flipped.

generalfeedback.text: At a=T,b=F,c=T, p = (T||F)&&T = T. Flipping a → (F||F)&&T = F (active); flipping c → (T||F)&&F = F (active); flipping b → (T||T)&&T = T (not active). So 2 clauses are active.

questiontext.text: What do the inactive clause coverage criteria (GICC/RICC) require?

answer.text: For each clause, tests where it does NOT determine the predicate, covering the cases it is true and false

feedback.text: Correct — inactive-clause coverage checks behaviour when the clause is masked out.

answer.text: For each clause, tests where it DOES determine the predicate

feedback.text: That is the active-clause family (GACC/CACC/RACC).
That is Combinatorial Coverage.

answer.text: Only that the predicate takes both values

feedback.text: That is Predicate Coverage.

generalfeedback.text: Inactive Clause Coverage requires, for each clause, tests in which it does not determine the predicate (it is "masked"), covering the situations where the clause is true and where it is false — the complement of the active-clause idea.

questiontext.text: Restricted Active Clause Coverage (RACC) subsumes Correlated Active Clause Coverage (CACC).

feedback.text: Correct — pinning the minor clauses equal (RACC) and having the major clause determine p forces p to differ, so CACC is satisfied.
RACC is strictly stronger: RACC → CACC → GACC.

generalfeedback.text: The active-clause hierarchy is RACC subsumes CACC subsumes GACC. RACC's identical-minor-clause requirement implies CACC's requirement that p differ across the test pair.

name.text: Determination of a in (a AND b) OR c

questiontext.text: For predicate p = (a ∧ b) ∨ c, clause a determines p exactly when:

answer.text: b is true and c is false

feedback.text: Correct — only then does p reduce to a.

answer.text: b is true and c is true

feedback.text: With c true, p is true regardless of a, so a does not determine p.

answer.text: b is false and c is false

feedback.text: With b false, a ∧ b is false regardless of a, so a does not determine p.

answer.text: b is false and c is true

feedback.text: c true fixes p true; also b false masks a. a does not determine p.

generalfeedback.text: a determines p only when the term a ∧ b passes a's value through (needs b = true) and the disjunction does not mask it (needs c = false). So a determines p exactly when b = true and c = false.

name.text: Active clause coverage subsumes clause coverage

questiontext.text: General Active Clause Coverage (GACC) subsumes Clause Coverage (CC).

feedback.text: Correct — GACC makes each clause both true and false (as the major clause of its pair), which is exactly what Clause Coverage requires.
GACC requires, for every clause, a true test and a false test, so every clause takes both values — Clause Coverage is satisfied.

generalfeedback.text: Every active-clause criterion requires each clause to be both true and false when it is the major clause, so all of GACC/CACC/RACC subsume Clause Coverage.

questiontext.text: CACC (and RACC) is infeasible for a clause that can never determine its predicate.

feedback.text: Correct — if no assignment of the other clauses ever lets that clause determine the predicate, no test can satisfy the active-clause requirement for it.
Determination is a precondition for active-clause coverage; without it the criterion's test requirement for that clause has no test that can satisfy it, so it is infeasible.

generalfeedback.text: Active-clause criteria (CACC, RACC, GACC) require a test pair where the clause determines the predicate. If some clause structurally never determines the predicate (e.g., it is masked out or redundant), that test requirement can never be satisfied — it is infeasible.

questiontext.text: Which DNF-based logic-coverage criterion requires every unique true point of the predicate to be covered? (acronym)

feedback.text: Correct.
Correct.

generalfeedback.text: Unique True Point Coverage (UTPC) requires, for each term in the predicate's DNF representation, a test that makes exactly that term true (and all others false) — the "unique" true point for that term.

questiontext.text: Modified Condition/Decision Coverage (MC/DC), as required by DO-178C, is essentially the same as which logic-coverage criterion?

feedback.text: Correct — MC/DC requires each clause to independently affect the decision outcome, which is CACC.
PC only requires the whole decision to take both values; MC/DC is much stronger.
CoC requires all 2^n combinations; MC/DC needs far fewer (n+1).
CC does not require each clause to independently determine the outcome.

generalfeedback.text: MC/DC demands that each clause be shown to independently affect the decision's outcome — exactly the active-clause / determination idea captured by CACC.

questiontext.text: A decision has 4 independent clauses. What is the minimum number of tests that can satisfy CACC (MC/DC)?

feedback.text: Correct — n+1 = 4+1 = 5.
8 = 2n is the upper bound, not the minimum.
16 = 2^4 is Combinatorial Coverage.
You need at least n+1 = 5 to show all four clauses independently affect the outcome.

generalfeedback.text: CACC/MC-DC for n independent clauses is achievable with a minimum of n+1 tests; for n = 4 that is 5.

name.text: Assignments where c determines the predicate

questiontext.text: For predicate p = (a ∧ b) ∨ c, in how many of the 8 assignments does clause c determine p?

feedback.text: Correct — c determines p whenever a ∧ b is false, which is 6 of the 8 rows.
a ∧ b is true in only 2 rows; c determines p in the other 6.
Recount — a ∧ b is false in 6 of 8 rows, and c determines p in each of those.
When a=T and b=T (2 rows), p is true regardless of c, so c does not determine p there.

generalfeedback.text: c determines p = (a ∧ b) ∨ c exactly when a ∧ b is false. a ∧ b is true in 2 rows (a=T,b=T) and false in 6, so c determines p in 6 assignments.

questiontext.text: A predicate uses clauses c1: x > 5 and c2: x < 0. Any test requirement needing c1 and c2 both true is:

answer.text: Infeasible — no single value of x makes both clauses true

feedback.text: Correct — the clauses are contradictory, so that combination cannot occur.

answer.text: Feasible with the right value of x

feedback.text: No x is both greater than 5 and less than 0.
No criterion can realise a semantically impossible combination.
Feasibility is about whether inputs exist, not about which criterion is used.

generalfeedback.text: Clauses can be logically dependent. Here c1 and c2 are mutually exclusive, so any requirement that both hold simultaneously is infeasible and must be excluded when measuring coverage.

questiontext.text: In the DNF (sum-of-products) view of a predicate, an implicant is:

answer.text: A product term (conjunction of literals) that, when true, makes the predicate true

feedback.text: Correct — an implicant implies the predicate.

answer.text: Any single clause of the predicate

feedback.text: An implicant is a product term of literals, not necessarily one clause.

answer.text: An assignment that makes the predicate false

feedback.text: An implicant makes the predicate true, not false.

answer.text: The disjunction of all product terms

feedback.text: That is the whole DNF; an implicant is one of its terms (or any term that implies f).

generalfeedback.text: An implicant is a conjunction of literals whose truth guarantees the predicate is true (it implies f). A DNF expresses f as a disjunction of implicants; a prime implicant is one from which no literal can be dropped.

questiontext.text: A unique true point for an implicant i of predicate f is an assignment that:

answer.text: Makes implicant i true and every other implicant of f false

feedback.text: Correct — only i is responsible for f being true there.

answer.text: Makes every implicant of f true

feedback.text: Then the point is not "unique" to i.
A true point makes f (and i) true.

answer.text: Is the only assignment that makes f true

feedback.text: Uniqueness is about which implicant is true, not about f having a single satisfying row.

generalfeedback.text: A unique true point for implicant i is an assignment where i is true and all other implicants are false, so i alone accounts for f being true — the basis of Unique True Point Coverage.

questiontext.text: For a clause c in implicant i, a near false point (used by CUTPNFP) is an assignment that:

answer.text: Makes f false and differs from a unique true point of i in exactly clause c

feedback.text: Correct — flipping c alone across the pair flips f, showing c's independent effect.

answer.text: Makes f true using implicant i

feedback.text: A near false point makes f false, not true.

answer.text: Makes every clause of i false

feedback.text: Only clause c differs from the true point; the other literals of i stay as they were.

answer.text: Differs from a true point in all clauses

feedback.text: It differs in exactly one clause, c, so it is "near".

generalfeedback.text: A near false point for clause c in implicant i makes f false while differing from a unique true point of i only in c. Pairing the two shows that toggling c alone changes f — the DNF analog of independent effect.

questiontext.text: The DNF criterion CUTPNFP (Corresponding Unique True Point and Near False Point Pair Coverage) is designed to:

answer.text: Emulate MC/DC in DNF form by pairing a unique true point with a near false point differing in one clause

feedback.text: Correct — the pair demonstrates each clause's independent effect on f.

answer.text: Cover all 2^n combinations of clause values

feedback.text: That is Combinatorial Coverage, not CUTPNFP.

answer.text: Guarantee only that the predicate takes both values

feedback.text: That is merely Predicate Coverage.
CUTPNFP is about showing each clause's active (independent) effect, not inactivity.

generalfeedback.text: CUTPNFP pairs, for each clause c of each implicant i, a unique true point of i with a near false point that differs only in c. Toggling c flips f, giving the DNF equivalent of MC/DC's independent-effect requirement.

questiontext.text: Among the clause/predicate logic criteria, which is the strongest (subsumes the others)?

feedback.text: Correct — exercising all 2^n combinations subsumes PC, CC, and every active/inactive-clause criterion.
CACC is strong but is subsumed by Combinatorial Coverage.
PC is one of the weakest logic criteria.
CC is weak and does not even subsume PC.

generalfeedback.text: Combinatorial Coverage requires every truth-value combination, so it subsumes all the other clause/predicate criteria (at the cost of exponential test count).

questiontext.text: Which ordering of the active-clause criteria is correct, from strongest (subsumes) to weakest?

feedback.text: Correct — RACC is the most restrictive, GACC the most permissive.
This reverses the order; RACC is the strongest.
RACC subsumes CACC, so RACC must come first.
GACC is the weakest, so it cannot lead the chain.

generalfeedback.text: RACC (identical minor clauses) subsumes CACC (p must differ) subsumes GACC (minor clauses free). Both RACC and CACC subsume Predicate Coverage; GACC does not.

questiontext.text: Which statement about subsumption of Predicate Coverage (PC) by the active-clause criteria is correct?

answer.text: CACC subsumes PC, but GACC does not

feedback.text: Correct — CACC forces p to take both values; GACC can leave p one-valued across a clause's test pair.

answer.text: Both CACC and GACC subsume PC

feedback.text: GACC does not require p to differ across the pair, so it need not satisfy PC.

answer.text: Neither CACC nor GACC subsumes PC

feedback.text: CACC does subsume PC because it requires p to take both values.

answer.text: GACC subsumes PC, but CACC does not

feedback.text: It is the other way around.

generalfeedback.text: CACC requires the predicate to be true in one test and false in the other of each pair, so it subsumes Predicate Coverage. GACC allows the minor clauses to differ so that the predicate can stay one-valued; a subtle counterexample shows GACC does not subsume PC.

questiontext.text: Implicant Coverage (IC) for a predicate in DNF requires that:

answer.text: Each implicant is made true by at least one test

feedback.text: Correct — every product term must be exercised as true.

answer.text: Each implicant is made true by a point where no other implicant is true

feedback.text: That stronger requirement is Unique True Point Coverage, not plain Implicant Coverage.

answer.text: Every clause takes both truth values

feedback.text: That is Clause Coverage, not an implicant-based criterion.
That is Combinatorial Coverage.

generalfeedback.text: Implicant Coverage requires each implicant (product term) of the DNF to be true in some test. UTPC strengthens this by demanding the point be unique to that implicant.

name.text: Assignments where a determines a 4-clause predicate

questiontext.text: For predicate p = (a ∧ b) ∨ (c ∧ d), in how many of the 16 assignments does clause a determine p?

feedback.text: Correct — a determines p when b is true and (c ∧ d) is false: 1 (b=T) × 3 (c ∧ d false of 4) × 2 (a free) = 6.
b=T gives 8 rows, but the 2 rows with c ∧ d also true must be removed, leaving 6.
Recount — there are 6 assignments where a determines p.
a cannot determine p when b is false (half the rows), so the count is well under 12.

generalfeedback.text: a determines p only when its term passes a through (b = true) and the other term does not mask it (c ∧ d false). That is 1 × 3 × 2 = 6 of the 16 assignments.
